strengths.quote: The absence of a route is a feature of the document’s attention, not a map of the event.
strengths.why: Chapter 6 sharply distinguishes documentary silence from historical simplicity in a memorable sentence.

strengths.quote: A rider can cross open ground quickly; an empire has to make messages arrive.
strengths.why: Chapter 7 compresses the transition from mobile conquest to administration with force and clarity.

strengths.quote: The proposal does not remove coercion from communication; it classifies and concentrates it.
strengths.why: Chapter 7 offers a specific, original account of how regular administration can redistribute rather than erase burdens.

weaknesses.quote: The relation between frontier mobility and aggression remains open, but it can be made more exact.
weaknesses.why: Chapter 6 enters a long concluding sequence after already developing the distinction at length, contributing to recap fatigue.

weaknesses.quote: What can be distinguished is more secure than what can be ranked.
weaknesses.why: Chapter 6 closes elegantly, but only after several near-equivalent syntheses of the same caution.

weaknesses.quote: The passage does not establish that the proposal was put into operation or that a station actually drew labour and animals from those units.
weaknesses.why: Chapter 7 responsibly marks uncertainty, yet repeated variants of 'does not establish' create a uniform, defensive cadence.

weaknesses.quote: A question remains where the proposal becomes policy
weaknesses.why: Chapter 7 reopens an implementation question that the preceding paragraphs have already raised repeatedly, delaying the ending.

chapterNotes.6: Substantively rich and internally well supported: the chapter connects Temüjin’s rise, Alcuin’s moral interpretation, Ögedei’s proposed posts, and later fragmentation. Its source distinctions are careful, but the latter half repeatedly restates the same mobility-versus-organisation thesis, and much of the Mongol discussion is repeated in Chapter 7.
chapterNotes.7: The conquest-to-administration progression is strong, and the post-station mechanism is explained concretely through keepers, horses, routes, political divisions, and burden. It carefully preserves the proposal/practice uncertainty, but reiterates that caveat and reprises substantial Chapter 6 material, weakening excerpt-level pacing.

strengths.quote: The absence of a route is a feature of the document’s attention, not a map of the event.
strengths.why: Chapter 6 makes an exact methodological point without inflating Alcuin’s letter into evidence it cannot supply.

strengths.quote: Faith supplied an explanatory vocabulary, but it also organised communication and assistance.
strengths.why: Chapter 6 moves beyond a simple belief-versus-material-action contrast and shows how the religious network did practical work.

strengths.quote: A rider can cross open ground quickly; an empire has to make messages arrive.
strengths.why: Chapter 7 gives the chapter’s conceptual turn a concise and engaging hinge.

strengths.quote: The proposed network translates distance into a series of exchanges governed by place, personnel, and horses.
strengths.why: Chapter 7 makes administrative incorporation concrete rather than leaving it as a generic abstraction.

weaknesses.quote: Temüjin’s history shows mobility within a process of alliance, subduing, and political incorporation.
weaknesses.why: Chapter 6 invokes a Mongol history that this version has not yet presented, making its synthesis depend on material deferred to Chapter 7.

weaknesses.quote: Ögedei’s proposal shows a ruler trying to regulate movement through stations and horses.
weaknesses.why: Chapter 6 similarly refers to an unexplained proposal before the source and mechanism are introduced.

weaknesses.quote: The source does not establish that communities were transformed into contributors to an operating system.
weaknesses.why: Chapter 7’s caution is sound, but 'operating system' is an anachronistic abstraction beside the otherwise concrete historical prose.

weaknesses.quote: A question remains where the proposal becomes policy
weaknesses.why: Chapter 7 starts a second ending and repeats the already established uncertainty about implementation.

chapterNotes.6: The Lindisfarne analysis is focused, specific, and alert to the difference between an observer’s moral meaning and the attackers’ unknown organisation. Deleting the earlier Mongol exposition greatly improves excerpt-level concision, but the final comparative synthesis now names Temüjin and Ögedei before this version has introduced their evidence, so the chapter’s progression is locally incomplete.
chapterNotes.7: This is the stronger chapter: it moves from genealogy and coalition to the concrete mechanics and burdens of proposed postal administration, then tests the distinction against conquest and fragmentation. Its caveats protect against unsupported certainty, though their repeated phrasing and the extended final questions still slow the close.

reason: B gives the better reading experience across the two-chapter excerpt because Chapter 7 no longer repeats a long Temüjin–Ögedei sequence already delivered in Chapter 6. It preserves the strongest substantive treatment of Alcuin, Temüjin, incorporation, postal administration, and the proposal-versus-practice uncertainty. The cost is real: B’s Chapter 6 concludes with comparative references to Temüjin and Ögedei before introducing them, whereas A supplies that scaffolding. A is therefore more self-contained at the chapter level, but its large-scale duplication and repeated recap loops outweigh that advantage.

materialDifferences.quote: He was born around 1160, according to the description of the work
materialDifferences.significance: B omits this approximate biographical date entirely; it is a discrete historical fact rather than merely duplicated framing.

materialDifferences.quote: And it is a suffering for the nation and the people.
materialDifferences.significance: A preserves this direct wording from Ögedei’s complaint in Chapter 6; B retains the burden in paraphrase in Chapter 7, so the explanation survives but the source’s emphatic language does not.

materialDifferences.quote: Temüjin is not placed at the head of an already unified people.
materialDifferences.significance: A establishes the fragmentation-and-incorporation frame before Chapter 6 compares Mongol and Lindisfarne evidence. B develops the idea fully in Chapter 7, but its Chapter 6 synthesis arrives without this local foundation.

remainingProblems: Both versions overuse repeated caveats built around what a passage 'does not establish,' producing a cautious but mechanically uniform rhythm.
Both versions retain a long Chapter 7 coda that restates the uncertainty over whether Ögedei’s proposal became consistent practice.
Version A duplicates major Temüjin, Ögedei, mobility, and fragmentation arguments across Chapters 6 and 7.
Version B’s Chapter 6 comparative ending depends on Mongol evidence that is introduced only in the following chapter.
